title: Investors Buy Your Judgment and Then Want a Say in It
summary: An investor or joint-venture partner gives you capital in exchange for a share of the outcome and a set of rights over the decisions that matter. JAX explains the four things every partnership agreement has to settle: who decides what, what the investors are told and when, how the sponsor’s interests are tied to theirs, and what happens if the sponsor has to be removed.
body:
When an investor puts money into your project, he is buying your judgment and accepting that you will run the day-to-day. In exchange he wants three things written down: the decisions he must approve, the information he will receive, and proof that you win only when he does.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between a term sheet and a commitment letter from a lender?

A. A term sheet is usually non-binding on the loan itself. A commitment letter is usually a binding offer to lend, subject to conditions precedent that must be met before funding.

Q. What is your best alternative to a negotiated agreement, and why does it matter?

A. It is the specific course you will take if no deal is reached. It sets how strong your hand is and is the source of your reservation price.

Q. Why does the choice between debt and equity matter when you finance your own structure?

A. Because interest may be deductible and repayable while equity returns are not, and tax rules may limit how much related-party debt is respected. The rules vary; verify against the primary source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the lenders of last week lend against the building. Equity investors and joint-venture partners own a piece of it, so they care not only whether the loan is paid but how every major choice is made. A developer who treats investors as a source of cash and nothing more will raise money once. A developer who gives them clear rights, honest reporting and real alignment will raise it again and again, often from the same people.

A joint venture, here, means a company or partnership owned by two or more parties to carry out one project or a set of projects. The party that finds, builds and manages the project is the sponsor or managing partner. The party that brings most of the money is the investor. The document that governs the relationship is the joint-venture or partnership agreement.

Who decides what: the major decisions list

In plain English: you run the project, but some decisions are too important for you to make alone.

The professional framing is the major decisions list: a defined set of actions that need the investor’s consent. Typical items include approving and changing the annual budget and business plan beyond a stated tolerance, borrowing or refinancing, selling the property, admitting new partners, entering contracts with the sponsor or its affiliates, starting or settling litigation above a threshold, and changing the project’s use. Everything not on the list stays with the sponsor. The thresholds are commercial terms, negotiated deal by deal.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. The approved budget is 30,000,000 dollars. The agreement says any increase above 3 percent of the budget, or any single change order above 500,000 dollars, is a major decision. A 400,000 dollar change order to upgrade the lobby does not need consent. A 900,000 dollar foundation redesign does. If cumulative changes reach 900,000 dollars, which is 3 percent of the budget, the next change needs consent whatever its size. Write the list tightly enough to protect the investor and loosely enough that you can still run a construction site.

What investors are told: reporting

Investors are entitled to know, on a schedule they can rely on, what is happening to their money. Typical reporting: a quarterly report with the budget against actual cost, the schedule, leasing or sales, cash on hand, loan status and any covenant tests; annual financial statements, often reviewed or audited by an independent accountant; and prompt notice of defined bad events, such as a covenant breach or a lawsuit. Agree the format and deadline before the money arrives. A report that is late or changes shape every quarter tells the investor more than its numbers do.

Say that out loud now.

How interests are tied together: alignment

Alignment means the sponsor does well only when the investor does well. Three tools create it. Co-investment: the sponsor puts its own money into the same equity, on the same terms, often 5 to 20 percent of the total as a matter of commercial practice. The promote, from Week 38: the sponsor’s extra share of profit paid only after investors clear a return hurdle. And fee discipline: fees that cover the sponsor’s real costs rather than becoming the main source of its profit.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Equity is 10,000,000 dollars. The sponsor co-invests 1,000,000 dollars. Its fees over the project total 1,320,000 dollars. If the project loses 20 percent of its equity, the sponsor loses 200,000 dollars on its co-investment but still keeps 1,320,000 dollars of fees. It is ahead while its investors lose money. That is misalignment, and investors who see it will either walk away or demand that part of the fees wait until they are repaid. JAX will put the full numbers on that on Day 3.

When the sponsor must go: removal

Finally, investors want a way to remove the sponsor if things go badly wrong. Removal for cause means removal for defined serious misconduct, such as fraud, wilful misconduct, gross negligence or a material uncured breach, and usually costs the sponsor its promote. Removal without cause, where it exists, is rarer and usually more expensive for the investor. Read the definitions closely: who decides that cause exists, and is there a cure period? A removal clause no one can ever trigger protects no one; a clause triggered by a minor breach makes the sponsor’s position impossible.

How the best do it

Experienced institutional investors usually start a joint venture with a business plan approved before closing, a major decisions list tied to that plan, quarterly reporting in a fixed template and an annual meeting to approve the next year’s budget. The sponsor knows in advance what it can do alone and what it must ask. A small developer can copy this with a two-page business plan, a one-page major decisions list and a reporting template agreed on day one.

Six-Lens Check

Tax. The choice of vehicle, partnership or company, decides how profit, fees and the promote are taxed for each partner; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Liability. The sponsor often carries duties to the investors and may give guarantees to lenders; know what each document makes you personally responsible for.

Banking. Lenders want to know who controls the borrower; major decisions and removal rights can trigger change-of-control clauses in the loan.

Governance. The major decisions list, reporting and removal clauses are the governance; write them before the money arrives, not after the first dispute.

Estate. Decide what happens to the sponsor’s interest and its role if a key person dies or is disabled.

Exit. Agree how and when either side can sell or force a sale, because investors need a door out before they will walk in.

Write the four answers on one page

Before the first investor meeting, write a single page with four headings: decisions, reporting, alignment, removal. Under each, write in plain sentences what you propose. Hand it over at the start of the meeting. It shows the investor you have thought about his protection before he asked, and it gives his lawyer a short list to negotiate instead of a long draft to fight.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is raising money on trust and handshakes, with no agreed list of who decides what. The first disagreement then becomes a dispute about authority. The control is a written major decisions list, reporting template and removal clause signed before the first dollar arrives.

The beginner's mistake

Promising investors everything to get them in, including consent rights over day-to-day decisions. The project then stalls every time a small change needs a signature from someone who is on holiday.

Callback

In Week 35, Omar and LEX taught minute books, resolutions and signing authority. A joint venture is the same discipline with two owners: every major decision becomes a written consent filed in the minute book, so that anyone, a lender, an auditor or a future buyer, can see that the decision was properly made.

Recap

Investors buy your judgment and want a say in the decisions that matter. Settle four things in writing: the major decisions list, reporting, alignment through co-investment, promote and fee discipline, and removal for cause.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: what happened when a celebrated founder’s governance met the public markets in 2019.
checklist: I have a written major decisions list with clear thresholds.
Everything not on that list stays with the sponsor, in writing.
Reporting format, frequency and deadline are agreed before closing.
My co-investment is on the same terms as the investors’.
I have tested whether I can profit from fees while investors lose money.
Removal for cause is defined, with who decides and a cure period.
I know how major decisions and removal affect the loan’s change-of-control terms.
Every major decision is recorded as a written consent in the minute book.
head: Field checklist
speak: When an investor joins my project, he is buying my judgment and accepting that I run the day-to-day. In return he needs four things in writing. First, a major decisions list: budget changes above a tolerance, borrowing, selling, new partners, related-party contracts, big litigation and changes of use need his consent, and everything else stays with me. Second, reporting: a fixed quarterly template with budget against actual, schedule, leasing, cash and loan tests, plus annual financial statements and prompt notice of bad events. Third, alignment: my own co-investment on the same terms, a promote paid only after investors clear their hurdle, and fees that cover my costs rather than becoming my profit. If I can earn fees while investors lose money, we are not aligned. Fourth, removal for cause, defined clearly, with who decides and a cure period. I agree all of it before the first dollar arrives.
terms: Major decision — an action defined in a joint-venture agreement that needs the investor’s consent before the sponsor can take it.
Co-investment — the sponsor’s own capital invested in the same equity, on the same terms, as its investors.
Removal for cause — the investors’ right to replace the sponsor for defined serious misconduct, usually with loss of the promote.

hostile.q: Your fees are paid whether or not we make money. Why should we believe you are aligned with us?
hostile.a: You should test it, not believe it. My co-investment is 10 percent of the equity on your terms, so I lose when you lose. My promote is paid only after you receive your capital and an 8 percent preferred return. And I propose that half of the development fee and all of the asset management fee wait behind your preferred return. If the project underperforms, I earn far less than my fees on paper. I can show you that in a table.

title: WeWork 2019: When Investors Could See Everything and Control Nothing
summary: In 2019 WeWork’s parent filed to go public, and the filing revealed related-party dealings and a voting structure that left investors with almost no control. Within weeks the offering was withdrawn and the founder stepped down. Ford and Cole trace how governance, not property, broke the deal.
rule: Rule 68: Disclose every related-party arrangement, put it to the investors for approval before it starts, and never give yourself control that no investor can check or remove.
body:
In 2019 WeWork’s parent company filed to sell shares to the public. The filing showed investors a founder with enormous control and a web of dealings between him and the company. Within about six weeks the offering was withdrawn and he had stepped down as chief executive. The buildings did not cause the collapse. Governance did.

Recall

Q. When sizing a loan, which limit decides the amount?

A. Whichever of the lender’s tests, coverage, loan to value, loan to cost or debt yield, produces the smallest loan.

Q. What was the root cause of the Stuyvesant Town loss in negotiation terms?

A. The price was set by the competition in an auction rather than by a written walk-away based on proven income.

Q. In concept, why do thin-capitalisation rules exist?

A. To limit how much interest on related-party debt a company can deduct, so that profits are not stripped out as interest. The tests vary; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this case is about the integrity of the relationship between a sponsor and his investors. WeWork was not a traditional developer; it leased space, fitted it out and rented it to others. But the failure was a governance failure that any real estate sponsor could repeat on a smaller scale: dealings with yourself, control no one can check, and investors who learn the truth late. The facts below are widely reported; where I am unsure of a figure, I describe it without the number.

1. Timeline

WeWork grew rapidly through the 2010s with large private investments, notably from SoftBank, and in early 2019 its private valuation was reported at about 47 billion dollars. In August 2019 its parent, then called The We Company, publicly filed its registration statement to sell shares. The filing disclosed, among other things, that the co-founder and chief executive, Adam Neumann, held shares with much greater voting power than ordinary shares; that the company had leased space in buildings in which he had ownership interests; that he had borrowed against his shares; and that the company had paid him about 5.9 million dollars for rights to the word “We,” a payment later reversed.

Investor reaction was severe, and the expected valuation fell sharply. On 24 September 2019 Mr Neumann stepped down as chief executive. On 30 September the company withdrew its offering. In October SoftBank agreed a rescue package. The company later listed through a merger in 2021 and filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States in November 2023.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered most: allowing the founder to transact with the company in his personal capacity, building a share structure that gave him control regardless of his economic stake, and taking that structure to public investors, who would read every line of it.

3. Assumptions

The structure assumed that investors valued growth and vision so highly that they would accept limited control and related-party dealings. Private investors had accepted them. The assumption was that public investors would too, and that disclosure would be a formality rather than a test.

Say that out loud now.

4. Incentives

Rapid growth raised the private valuation, which rewarded both the founder and early investors on paper. Related-party leases and loans gave the founder personal income streams separate from the company’s results. Investors who had bought in at high valuations had an incentive to support a public listing at an even higher one. Nobody in that chain was rewarded for slowing down and fixing governance.

5. Warning signs ignored

Related-party leases are a classic warning sign, because the founder sits on both sides of the rent. Control that cannot be challenged means there is no one to say no. A payment to the chief executive for a trademark the company was already using is the kind of transaction an independent board would ask about immediately. And losses were large relative to revenue, which meant that confidence in leadership was carrying more of the valuation than results were.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the public filing. Once the structure was disclosed to the public markets, it could not be quietly renegotiated. The company changed governance terms in response, but by then the investors’ view of the leadership had formed, and the offering could not proceed.

7. Root cause

The root cause was governance designed around the founder rather than around the investors: related-party dealings without independent approval, and control without accountability. Disclosure did not cause the failure; it revealed it.

Cole's view: what an auditor reads in a sponsor’s related-party list

Cole here. When I review a joint venture, I ask for one schedule first: every arrangement between the sponsor, its family or its affiliates and the project. Leases, loans, fees, management contracts, construction contracts, consulting. For each one I want the price, how it was set, who approved it and whether that person was independent of the sponsor.

A worked example, hypothetical. A sponsor’s own construction company builds the project for 24,000,000 dollars. The agreement requires investor approval of related-party contracts, and the sponsor obtained it after showing two independent bids at 24,500,000 and 25,000,000 dollars. That is a clean related-party contract: disclosed, competitively tested and independently approved. Now change one fact: no bids, no approval, and a fee of 4 percent on top. The same building becomes an audit finding and, possibly, a claim by the investors.

What a disciplined sponsor would have done

Ford again. Four habits, each cheap. First, keep a related-party schedule from the first day and update it every quarter, so that disclosure is routine rather than an event. Second, send every related-party arrangement to an independent approver before it starts: investors, an independent director or a committee with no stake in it. Third, price each one against independent evidence, such as bids, quotes or a valuation, and keep that evidence in the file. Fourth, design control so that someone can say no: a board with independent members, or investor consent rights on the decisions that matter, and a removal clause that can actually be used.

A worked example, hypothetical. A sponsor owns the land next to the project personally and wants to lease it to the venture for parking at 120,000 dollars a year. He discloses it, obtains two market quotes from car park operators at 110,000 and 130,000 dollars, and asks the investors to approve a five-year lease at 120,000 dollars with an independent rent review at year three. They approve it in a signed consent. The same lease, signed without disclosure, would be the first item in any investor’s claim. The money is identical; the process is everything.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk for a sponsor is dealing with your own project without disclosure and independent approval, because it destroys trust even when the price is fair. The control is Rule 68: disclose every related-party arrangement, get investor approval before it starts, and never hold control no one can check.

The beginner's mistake

Believing a related-party deal is fine because the price is reasonable. Investors judge the process as well as the price; an undisclosed fair deal looks exactly like an undisclosed unfair one.

Callback

In Week 61, Cole taught arm’s length pricing for intercompany fees. The same test applies here: a related-party contract must be priced as if between strangers and documented so that someone else can confirm it. Transfer pricing protects you from the tax authority; Rule 68 protects you from your own investors.

Recap

A public filing in 2019 revealed related-party dealings and a voting structure that gave investors little control. The offering was withdrawn and the founder stepped down within weeks. The root cause was governance built around one person. Rule 68: disclose, get approval and stay removable.

Next: JAX on The Money: fees, promote and whether the sponsor really wins only when investors do.
checklist: I keep a schedule of every related-party arrangement with the project.
Each one is priced against independent quotes or market evidence.
Each one is approved by investors before it starts.
No single person, including me, holds control that investors cannot check.
Removal and replacement rights are defined and workable.
Every disclosure I make to investors is complete, not selective.
I would be comfortable if every arrangement were read aloud to a new investor.
head: Field checklist
speak: In 2019 WeWork’s parent filed to go public. The filing disclosed that its co-founder held shares with far greater voting power than ordinary shareholders, that the company leased space in buildings he had interests in, that he had borrowed against his shares, and that the company had paid him about 5.9 million dollars for the word “We,” later reversed. Investors reacted badly, he stepped down as chief executive on 24 September, and the offering was withdrawn on 30 September. The root cause was governance built around one person: related-party dealings without independent approval and control without accountability. For a developer the lesson is direct. If my own construction company builds the project, I show competing bids and get investor approval first. Rule 68: disclose every related-party arrangement, get approval before it starts, and never give myself control that no investor can check or remove.
terms: Related-party transaction — an arrangement between a company and its sponsor, managers, their families or affiliates.
Registration statement — the disclosure document filed with a securities regulator before shares are offered to the public.
Dual-class shares — a share structure in which one class carries more votes per share than another, separating control from economic ownership.

hostile.q: Your construction company is building the project. How do we know you are not overcharging us?
hostile.a: Because you do not have to take my word for it. Before we signed, we obtained two independent bids, which you have, and our contract price is below both. The agreement requires your approval of any related-party contract and any change order above the threshold, and our cost consultant reports to you directly. If you would like your own consultant to review the contract, I will pay for it.

title: Fees Versus Promote: Does the Sponsor Win Only When Investors Win?
summary: A sponsor is paid in fees, a promote and returns on its own co-investment. JAX puts hypothetical numbers on a good and a bad outcome to show when fees make the sponsor indifferent to results, and how deferring or subordinating fees restores alignment.
body:
Count what the sponsor earns in a good year and in a bad one. If the difference is small because fees dominate, the sponsor is not aligned with his investors, whatever the agreement says. Move part of the fees behind the investors’ return and the alignment becomes real.

Recall

Q. On a lender’s late re-trade, what is the first question to ask?

A. What changed: something about our building, or the lender’s view of the market. The answer tells you what trade will work.

Q. How do you price a request for an early non-refundable deposit?

A. As an expected cost: the chance you will walk before the risk is known, times the deposit.

Q. Why might related-party debt be less tax-efficient than it looks?

A. Because interest deductions may be limited by thin-capitalisation or interest-limitation rules, and withholding may apply to interest paid abroad. Verify against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, on Day 1 I told you that alignment means the sponsor wins only when the investors win. Today we test that with numbers, because investors will. A sophisticated investor reads your fee schedule before your pro forma, and asks one question: in a bad case, how much does the sponsor still earn? All figures are hypothetical.

The deal

Total project cost is 30,000,000 dollars, with 20,000,000 dollars of debt and 10,000,000 dollars of equity. The sponsor co-invests 1,000,000 dollars, 10 percent of the equity, on the same terms as investors. The waterfall pays all equity an 8 percent preferred return, compounded annually, then splits the remaining profit 80 percent to equity and 20 percent to the sponsor as its promote. For simplicity the promote is computed on the whole equity, and there is no catch-up. The project lasts three years.

The fees: an acquisition fee of 1 percent of total cost, 300,000 dollars; a development fee of 3 percent of hard and soft costs of 24,000,000 dollars, 720,000 dollars; and an asset management fee of 1 percent of equity a year, 300,000 dollars over three years. Total fees: 1,320,000 dollars.

The good case

The project sells after three years and returns 16,000,000 dollars to equity, a profit of 6,000,000 dollars. The preferred return on 10,000,000 dollars at 8 percent for three years, compounded, is about 2,597,000 dollars. Profit above the hurdle is about 3,403,000 dollars. The promote is 20 percent of that, about 681,000 dollars.

The sponsor’s total: 1,320,000 dollars of fees, about 681,000 dollars of promote, plus its share of the equity return on its 1,000,000 dollar co-investment, roughly 530,000 dollars after the promote. About 2,530,000 dollars in all.

Say that out loud now.

The bad case

Costs overrun and the market softens. The project returns 11,000,000 dollars to equity, a profit of 1,000,000 dollars, about a 3 percent annual return, below the 8 percent hurdle. The promote is zero. The sponsor still earns all 1,320,000 dollars of fees, plus about 100,000 dollars on its co-investment. About 1,420,000 dollars in all.

Compare the two. Investors’ profit fell from about 4,800,000 dollars to about 900,000 dollars, a fall of more than 80 percent. The sponsor’s earnings fell from about 2,530,000 dollars to about 1,420,000 dollars, a fall of about 44 percent. Fees cushioned the sponsor far more than the investors. That is the number a careful investor will put in front of you.

Restoring alignment: a second worked example

Now change the fee terms. Half the development fee, 360,000 dollars, is deferred until investors receive their capital plus the preferred return. The asset management fee, 300,000 dollars, is subordinated: it accrues but is paid only after the preferred return. In the good case nothing changes; the hurdle is cleared and all fees are paid. In the bad case, the hurdle is not cleared, so 660,000 dollars of fees are not paid, or are paid only from whatever is left after investors receive their preferred return. The sponsor’s bad-case earnings fall to about 760,000 dollars: 660,000 dollars of fees plus about 100,000 dollars on its co-investment.

Now the sponsor’s earnings fall about 70 percent in the bad case, much closer to the investors’ fall. That is real alignment, and it is the trade that wins investors who have seen many fee schedules. It also costs you less than it seems in a project you believe in, because in the good case you are paid in full.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

Warrick here. On your personal balance sheet, fees are income you receive during the project, while promote and co-investment are assets whose value is uncertain until exit. A sponsor who lives on fees can grow a business; a sponsor whose wealth is mostly promote is concentrated in his own deals. Track both, and decide how much of your net worth you are willing to hold in projects you control. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

Personal brand thread: reputation with investors

This month’s thread is personal brand. With investors, your brand is not your logo or your website. It is the fee schedule you propose, how quickly you report bad news, and whether your first project returned what you said it would. An investor who receives an honest, early warning about an overrun remembers it longer than one who received a glossy report.

Ask yourself: if an investor called the people who backed my last project, what would they say about how I behaved when things went wrong? Write down the answer you would want, and then act so that it is true.

A third worked example: the catch-up question

Some waterfalls add a catch-up: after investors receive their preferred return, the sponsor receives most or all of the next distributions until it has its full share of total profit, and only then do the 80 to 20 splits resume. In the good case here, a full catch-up would give the sponsor 20 percent of the whole 6,000,000 dollar profit, 1,200,000 dollars, instead of about 681,000 dollars. That is about 519,000 dollars more, all of it paid in the good case. A catch-up therefore strengthens the sponsor’s reward for success without paying it more for failure, which is why investors examine it closely and why it is a negotiated term, not a standard one. If you ask for a catch-up, be ready to give something on fees in exchange, and show the investor both cases in the same table.

Showing investors the table

Put the good case and the bad case side by side for both the sponsor and the investors: total received, profit, and percentage change between cases. Hand it over before the investor asks. An investor who sees that you modelled your own downside honestly is more likely to trust the rest of your pro forma.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a fee structure that lets the sponsor do well while investors do badly, which destroys trust and the next raise. The control is to model both cases and defer or subordinate enough fees to make the sponsor’s bad case hurt.

The beginner's mistake

Comparing your fees with market averages and stopping there. Investors care less about whether each fee is standard than about whether, in total, you are paid for results.

Callback

In Week 38, JAX and Elias taught preferred return, catch-up and promote. Today showed the same waterfall from the investor’s side of the table: the promote rewards performance, but only if the fees beside it do not already pay the sponsor for showing up.

Recap

Model the sponsor’s earnings in a good and a bad case. If fees cushion the sponsor far more than investors, defer part of the development fee and subordinate the asset management fee behind the preferred return. Your brand with investors is how you behave when the bad case happens.

Next: Omar on The Rules: duties, consents and the law that governs a joint venture.
checklist: I modelled my total earnings in a good case and a bad case.
I compared the percentage fall in my earnings with the investors’.
My co-investment is on the same terms as the investors’.
Part of my development fee is deferred behind the preferred return.
My asset management fee is subordinated in a bad case.
I track fees as income and promote as an uncertain asset on my ledger.
I report bad news to investors early and in writing.
head: Field checklist
speak: I test alignment with numbers. On a 30,000,000 dollar project with 10,000,000 dollars of equity, my fees total 1,320,000 dollars, and my promote is 20 percent of profit above an 8 percent preferred return. In a good case, with 6,000,000 dollars of profit, I earn about 2,530,000 dollars in fees, promote and co-investment return. In a bad case, with 1,000,000 dollars of profit, the promote is zero but I still earn about 1,420,000 dollars. Investors’ profit falls by more than 80 percent; mine falls by about 44 percent. That is misalignment. So I defer half the development fee and subordinate the asset management fee behind the preferred return. Then my bad-case earnings fall to about 760,000 dollars, a fall of about 70 percent, much closer to the investors’. In the good case I am paid in full. And I remember that my brand with investors is how I behave when the bad case arrives.
terms: Fee deferral — an agreement that part of a sponsor’s fee is paid only after investors receive defined returns.
Subordinated fee — a fee that accrues but is paid only after investors’ capital and preferred return, so it is at risk in a bad case.
Preferred return — the return investors receive before the sponsor shares in profit, a negotiated hurdle rather than a guarantee.

hostile.q: Your fees add up to more than your promote even in your own good case. Are you a developer or a fee collector?
hostile.a: Fair question. In the good case, the fees cover a team that works on this project for three years, and the promote and my co-investment are my reward for results. To make sure I am not paid for showing up, I have proposed that 660,000 dollars of the fees wait behind your preferred return. In the bad case my earnings fall by about 70 percent, close to yours. I can show you the table for both cases.

title: Duties, Consents and Conflicts: The Law Inside a Joint Venture
summary: A joint venture is governed by the law of the vehicle and by the agreement the partners sign. Omar explains, as concepts, the duties a sponsor may owe investors, how agreements can shape those duties, how related-party conflicts are approved, and what information rights investors hold. Law varies by place; verify every point.
body:
The joint-venture agreement is not the only law that governs your relationship with investors. The law of the vehicle may impose duties of loyalty and care, and the agreement decides how far those duties can be shaped. Know both before you sign, because a sponsor who misunderstands his duties can lose his promote and more.

Recall

Q. What is the comparison grid used for in a lender process?

A. To set every lender’s price and structure terms side by side, so you compare the loans you would actually live with rather than their headline rates.

Q. What is misrepresentation in a negotiation?

A. A false statement of fact made before a contract that induces the other side to enter it, which can allow the deal to be undone or damages claimed.

Q. In concept, what does a thin-capitalisation rule look at?

A. The ratio of a company’s related-party debt to its equity, or its interest to its earnings, to limit deductible interest. Verify the tests against the primary source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, investors usually sign a long agreement and assume it is the whole story. Sponsors often assume the same. But in many systems, a person who manages money or property for others can owe duties the agreement does not mention, and breaching them can make the sponsor liable personally. This lesson is concepts, not advice. The rules depend on the vehicle, partnership, limited partnership, company or limited liability company, and on the place. Verify every point against the primary source before you rely on it.

Fiduciary duty: loyalty and care

In plain English: if you manage someone else’s money, the law may require you to put their interests ahead of your own in the matters you manage, and to act carefully.

The professional framing is fiduciary duty: a duty owed by a person in a position of trust, typically including a duty of loyalty, meaning no undisclosed conflicts and no secret profits, and a duty of care, meaning reasonable diligence. Directors of companies and general partners of partnerships often owe such duties. In some jurisdictions and for some vehicles, the agreement can narrow or define these duties; in others it cannot remove them entirely [unverified — confirm independently]. Never assume a clause in the agreement has removed your duties; ask your lawyer what the law of the vehicle allows.

A worked example, hypothetical. As general partner, you learn of a second site next door, ideal for the project’s phase two. You buy it personally and plan to sell it to the partnership later at a profit. If you owe a duty of loyalty, that may be a corporate opportunity that belonged to the partnership, and the profit may have to be handed over. The control: disclose the opportunity and let the investors decide, in writing, before you act.

Conflicts and related-party approval

Rule 68 told you to disclose every related-party arrangement and get approval before it starts. The law often requires the same, and the agreement should say exactly how. A good clause defines a related party, requires disclosure of the material terms, requires approval by the investors or by a committee with no interest in the arrangement, and allows the investors to engage their own adviser at the project’s cost. Approval given on incomplete information may not protect you.

A second worked example. You want your property management company to manage the building at 4 percent of revenue. You disclose the contract, show three market quotes at 3.5 to 4.5 percent, and the investors approve it in a signed consent. Two years later an investor complains. You have the disclosure, the quotes and the consent in the minute book. That file is your defence.

Say that out loud now.

Information rights

Investors usually hold information rights: the contractual and sometimes statutory right to receive reports and to inspect books and records. The agreement should set the regular reports and deadlines, the right to ask for further information, and how confidential material is handled. In many places, partners or shareholders have some inspection rights by law even if the agreement says nothing. Refusing a reasonable request is a fast way to turn a question into a dispute.

Consents that bind the vehicle

Major decisions require consent, but the agreement must also say how consent is given: in writing, by whom, within what time, and what happens if an investor does not respond. A deemed-consent clause, which treats silence after a stated period as approval, keeps the project moving. Without one, a single unresponsive investor can stop a refinancing. Record every consent in the minute book, as Omar and LEX taught in Week 35, so that a lender or buyer can rely on it.

A third worked example: the standard of conduct clause

Many agreements define a standard of conduct: the sponsor is not liable to investors for losses unless they result from fraud, wilful misconduct, gross negligence or a material breach of the agreement. Suppose, hypothetically, the sponsor chose a contractor that later became insolvent, costing the project 800,000 dollars. If the sponsor checked the contractor’s finances, obtained bonds and followed the approved procurement process, the clause will usually protect him; an honest decision that turned out badly is not gross negligence. If the sponsor skipped the checks because the contractor was a friend, the investors may argue gross negligence or a conflict, and the clause may not protect him. What separates the two outcomes is the file: the financial checks, the bond, the approvals and the conflict disclosure.

Indemnities and insurance for the sponsor

Agreements often require the venture to indemnify the sponsor for claims arising from its role, except where the standard of conduct is breached, and may allow the venture to buy liability insurance for its managers. Read both. An indemnity from a venture that has lost its money is worth little, and insurance often excludes exactly the claims investors bring. Ask your lawyer and your insurance broker what is actually covered before you rely on either.

Keeping the governance file

Keep one file for the venture’s governance: the agreement and amendments, the business plan, every consent, every related-party disclosure with its evidence, every information request and your answer, and the minutes of every investor meeting. If there is ever a dispute, the side with the better file usually has the easier argument.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is acting on a conflict, such as buying a neighbouring site or awarding yourself a contract, without disclosure and approval, because it can cost you the profit, the promote and your position. The control is a written conflict process followed every time, with the evidence kept.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming the agreement is the whole law. The law of the vehicle can add duties and inspection rights, and some of them cannot be signed away.

Callback

In Week 21, LEX and Omar taught agency and limited liability. A sponsor managing a joint venture is an agent for the investors in many respects, and an agent who profits secretly from his position is the classic breach. Limited liability protects the investors’ other assets; it does not protect a sponsor who breaches his own duties. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in the law of the vehicle, before you sign a joint-venture agreement.

Recap

A sponsor may owe duties of loyalty and care under the law of the vehicle, which the agreement may shape but not always remove. Disclose and approve conflicts with a written process. Respect information rights. Define how consent is given, including deemed consent, and record every consent.

Next: Nadia on The Numbers: reverse engineering an investor report to check whether the promote was paid correctly.
checklist: I know which duties the law of the vehicle imposes on me.
I know which duties the agreement can and cannot change.
I disclose every corporate opportunity before acting on it.
Related-party contracts have quotes, disclosure and a signed consent on file.
I respond to investor information requests promptly.
The agreement defines how consent is given, including deemed consent.
A lawyer qualified in the law of the vehicle reviewed the agreement.
head: Field checklist
speak: A joint-venture agreement is not the whole law. Depending on the vehicle and the place, a sponsor who manages investors’ money may owe fiduciary duties: loyalty, meaning no undisclosed conflicts or secret profits, and care, meaning reasonable diligence. Some agreements can narrow those duties; some cannot remove them, so I ask my lawyer what the law of the vehicle allows. If I find a neighbouring site the partnership could use, I disclose it and let the investors decide before I act. Every related-party contract gets disclosure, market quotes and a signed consent in the minute book. Investors hold information rights, some by contract and some by law, and I answer reasonable requests promptly. The agreement must say how consent is given and whether silence counts as consent after a set period, so one slow investor cannot stop a refinancing.
terms: Fiduciary duty — a duty owed by a person in a position of trust, typically including loyalty and care toward those they act for.
Corporate opportunity — a business opportunity that, because of a fiduciary’s role, may belong to the entity rather than to the fiduciary personally.
Deemed consent — a clause treating an investor’s silence after a stated period as approval of a proposed decision.

hostile.q: You bought the lot next door in your own name last year. Why should that not belong to the partnership?
hostile.a: I disclosed the opportunity to all investors in writing before I bought it, and offered it to the partnership at the same price. The investors declined in a signed consent, which is in the minute book, because it did not fit the business plan at the time. I can send you both documents today. If the partnership now wants it, I will offer it at my cost plus carrying costs, subject to an independent valuation.

title: Reverse Engineering an Investor Report
summary: Nadia starts from a finished investor report showing exit distributions and a promote, and works backward to test whether the investors received their preferred return first and whether the promote was calculated correctly. All numbers are hypothetical and rounded.
body:
An investor report states what was paid. Working backward from those payments, you can rebuild the preferred return, find what the promote should have been and see whether anyone was overpaid. If you cannot rebuild it, neither can your investors, and they will notice.

Recall

Q. What belongs on a joint venture’s major decisions list?

A. Actions too important for the sponsor alone, such as budget changes above a tolerance, borrowing, selling, new partners, related-party contracts, large litigation and changes of use.

Q. How do you find your walk-away land price from a pro forma?

A. Divide stabilised net operating income by your required yield on cost to get the maximum total cost, then subtract all non-land costs.

Q. What makes an intercompany loan defensible?

A. A written agreement, an arm’s length rate, a repayment schedule, actual payments that match it, and records showing both sides treat it as debt.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the waterfall in a joint-venture agreement is often clear in words and easy to get wrong in a spreadsheet. A missed compounding period or a promote calculated before the hurdle is cleared can move hundreds of thousands of dollars between the sponsor and investors. Investors’ accountants rebuild the numbers backward from the payments. You should do it first. This is an even week, so we start from the finished report.

The finished report

All figures are hypothetical. An investor group contributed 9,000,000 dollars at the start. The agreement gives investors an 8 percent preferred return, compounded annually, and their capital back, before the sponsor receives any promote. Above that, remaining distributions are split 80 percent to investors and 20 percent to the sponsor. The sponsor’s own co-investment is accounted for separately and is ignored here. The year-three report states: distribution in year two, 600,000 dollars to investors; exit distribution available in year three, 12,800,000 dollars; paid to investors 12,200,000 dollars; promote paid to sponsor 600,000 dollars.

Step 1: rebuild what investors were owed before any promote

Start with 9,000,000 dollars. After one year at 8 percent, the balance owed is 9,720,000 dollars. After two years, 10,497,600 dollars. Subtract the 600,000 dollar distribution in year two: 9,897,600 dollars. Grow it one more year at 8 percent: about 10,689,400 dollars. That is what investors had to receive at exit, capital plus preferred return, before the sponsor earned anything.

Step 2: find the amount above the hurdle

The exit distribution available was 12,800,000 dollars. Subtract the 10,689,400 dollars owed to investors. About 2,110,600 dollars remains above the hurdle. That is the amount to be split 80 to 20.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3: what should each side have received?

The sponsor’s 20 percent of 2,110,600 dollars is about 422,100 dollars. The investors’ 80 percent is about 1,688,500 dollars. So investors should have received 10,689,400 plus 1,688,500 dollars, about 12,377,900 dollars, and the sponsor about 422,100 dollars.

Compare with the report. Investors received 12,200,000 dollars, about 177,900 dollars too little. The sponsor received 600,000 dollars, about 177,900 dollars too much. The two errors match, which tells you the total was right and the split was wrong.

Step 4: find the cause

Look for the usual errors. One is computing the preferred return as simple interest instead of compounding: 8 percent of 9,000,000 dollars for three years, simple, is 2,160,000 dollars, which ignores the year-two distribution and the compounding. Another is calculating the promote on total profit instead of profit above the hurdle. Another is treating the year-two distribution as a return of profit rather than reducing the balance owed. Here, if the spreadsheet ignored the year-two distribution in the hurdle and then applied the split to a larger amount, the promote rises. Whatever the cause, write it down, correct the payment, and tell investors in writing what happened and how you fixed it.

A second worked example: the investors’ return

Investors put in 9,000,000 dollars, received 600,000 dollars in year two and, once corrected, about 12,377,900 dollars in year three. Their internal rate of return (IRR), the discount rate at which those payments have a present value of zero, is about 13.2 percent. With the uncorrected 12,200,000 dollars, it was about 12.7 percent. Half a point of IRR is exactly the kind of difference an investor’s accountant finds, and once found, it becomes a question about every other number you have reported.

A third worked example: when the hurdle is not met

Now suppose the exit cash available was only 10,400,000 dollars, below the 10,689,400 dollars owed to investors. There is nothing above the hurdle, so the promote is zero. Every dollar goes to investors, who receive 10,400,000 dollars and fall short of their preferred return by about 289,400 dollars. Whether that shortfall survives as a claim against anything else depends on the agreement; usually a preferred return is a priority, not a guarantee, and once the project’s cash is distributed there is nothing more to pay. Check what the agreement says, and say it plainly in the report: the preferred return was not fully met, by how much, and why.

Run this case before the exit, not after. If the forecast exit cash is close to the hurdle, the sponsor’s incentive changes, because the promote is worth nothing unless the project clears it. That is when investors watch most closely for a sponsor taking extra risk to reach the hurdle, and when clear reporting matters most.

The sponsor’s own checklist before paying a promote

Five checks, in order. One: confirm every contribution and distribution, with its date, against the bank statements, not the spreadsheet. Two: roll the hurdle forward using the exact compounding the agreement specifies, annual, quarterly or daily. Three: compute the amount above the hurdle from actual cash available, after reserves and costs. Four: apply the split, and any catch-up, exactly as written. Five: send the calculation to an independent accountant and to the investors before the payment, not with it. A promote paid after those five checks is a reward; paid without them, it is a risk.

Matching the report to the bank

Every figure in the investor report should trace to a bank statement or a signed document. If one cannot, mark it as an estimate in the report. Investors forgive estimates labelled honestly; they do not forgive estimates presented as facts.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is paying a promote before checking the waterfall backward from the actual payments, because an overpayment to yourself looks like self-dealing even when it is an arithmetic mistake. The control: before any promote is paid, rebuild the hurdle from cash flows and have someone other than the sponsor check it.

The beginner's mistake

Building the waterfall forward from the pro forma and never reconciling it to the actual dates and amounts of every distribution.

Callback

In Week 12, Nadia taught owner accounting: accrual, capitalised costs and reporting. The investor report is the end of that chain. If the books record each contribution and distribution on its real date, the waterfall can be rebuilt in minutes. If they do not, nobody can prove what anyone is owed.

Recap

Roll the investors’ capital forward at the preferred rate, subtracting each distribution on its date. Subtract that balance from the exit cash to find the amount above the hurdle, split it, and compare with what was paid. Find the cause of any difference, correct it and disclose it.

Next: JAX on The Room: the quarterly investor meeting with bad news and a request for consent.
checklist: I rolled investor capital forward at the preferred rate, compounding as the agreement says.
I subtracted each distribution on its actual date.
I computed the amount above the hurdle from actual exit cash.
I split that amount and compared it with what was paid.
I checked that overpayment and underpayment match.
I identified and wrote down the cause of any error.
Someone other than the sponsor checked the calculation before payment.
head: Field checklist
speak: I check an investor report backward. Investors put in 9,000,000 dollars with an 8 percent compounding preferred return. Rolled forward two years, they are owed about 10,497,600 dollars; subtract the 600,000 dollar year-two distribution and grow it one more year, and they are owed about 10,689,400 dollars at exit before any promote. The exit cash was 12,800,000 dollars, so about 2,110,600 dollars sat above the hurdle. Split 80 to 20, the sponsor should have received about 422,100 dollars and investors about 12,377,900 dollars. The report paid the sponsor 600,000 dollars and investors 12,200,000, so the sponsor was overpaid by about 177,900 dollars. The usual causes are simple interest instead of compounding, ignoring an interim distribution, or applying the promote to total profit. I find the cause, correct the payment and tell investors in writing before anyone else finds it.
terms: Hurdle — the return investors must receive, usually capital plus preferred return, before the sponsor’s promote begins.
Compounding — calculating a return on both the original amount and returns already accrued, period by period.
Internal rate of return (IRR) — the discount rate at which the present value of all cash flows in and out equals zero.

hostile.q: Our accountant says you paid yourself about 178,000 dollars too much promote. Was that a mistake or a choice?
hostile.a: It was a mistake, and your accountant is right. Our spreadsheet did not reduce the hurdle balance for the year-two distribution before applying the split. I have recalculated it from the actual cash flows, the overpayment is about 177,900 dollars, and I will return it to the investors within ten days. I will also send you the corrected calculation and have an independent accountant review the waterfall before any future promote is paid.

title: The Quarterly Meeting With Bad News and a Request for Consent
summary: A cost overrun has pushed the budget past the major-decision threshold, and you must tell investors and ask for their consent at the quarterly meeting. JAX gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question and how to hold your state.
body:
Bad news delivered early, with a cause, a plan and a request, builds more trust than good news delivered late. In the room, lead with the number, own the cause, offer a choice and stop talking.

Recall

Q. What does Rule 68 say?

A. Disclose every related-party arrangement, put it to the investors for approval before it starts, and never give yourself control that no investor can check or remove.

Q. In a landowner meeting, when should you stay silent?

A. After you state your number and its reason, and while the family confers among themselves.

Q. When presenting a structure with shareholder loans to a banker, what should you have ready?

A. The loan agreements, the rate and how it was set, the repayment record and how the loans rank behind the bank’s debt.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every project has a quarter where the news is bad. How you handle that meeting decides whether your investors back your next project. Investors do not expect perfection. They expect to hear the truth from you first, to understand what happened, and to be asked properly when the agreement says they must decide.

The scene

All figures are hypothetical. A 30,000,000 dollar project is halfway through construction. The structural steel package came in 1,500,000 dollars over budget because of a design change and a supplier price increase. Contingency can absorb 600,000 dollars. The remaining 900,000 dollars takes the budget 3 percent over the approved figure, which is a major decision requiring investor consent. You have three options: fund it from additional equity in proportion to ownership; increase the loan, which the lender has said it will consider; or cut finishes to save 500,000 dollars and fund the rest. Six investors are on the call.

The question behind the question

When an investor asks, “How did this happen?”, the question behind it is: did you know earlier, and are you telling us everything now? When an investor asks, “What else could go wrong?”, the question behind it is: can we still trust the rest of your numbers? Answer the stated question and then answer the real one.

The lines to say

Lead with the bottom line. “The steel package is 1,500,000 dollars over budget. Contingency covers 600,000. We need your consent for the remaining 900,000, which takes us 3 percent over the approved budget.”

Own the cause. “Two-thirds of it comes from a design change we approved in March to meet the fire engineer’s requirements; one-third is a supplier price increase. I should have flagged the design change’s cost risk to you in the March report, and I did not. That is on me.”

Offer a choice, with numbers. “There are three ways to fund it. Additional equity costs each of you your share of 900,000 dollars and keeps the loan unchanged. A larger loan avoids new equity but reduces our coverage headroom from about 8 percent to about 5 percent. Cutting finishes saves 500,000 dollars and may reduce rents slightly. Our recommendation is the larger loan plus 200,000 dollars of finish savings. Here is the table.”

Tell them what changes next. “From this quarter, every change order above 250,000 dollars will be reported to you within a week, not at quarter-end.”

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never say, “This is normal in construction,” even if it is; it sounds like an excuse. Never blame the contractor or the engineer by name in front of investors before the facts are settled. Never say, “We will make it up later,” without a plan that shows how. Never present the request as a formality: “We just need you to sign this.” The agreement made it their decision, and treating it otherwise breaches the trust Rule 68 protects. And never reveal one investor’s position to the others without permission.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after you state the number. Let them react. Stay silent again after you present the options and your recommendation; the investors need to talk, and your silence tells them the decision is genuinely theirs. If one investor is angry, let him finish before you respond.

Holding your state

Prepare the night before: the number, the cause, the three options, your recommendation, the table. If you are coming off a night shift, schedule the call for a time you are rested. In the meeting, speak slowly, keep your answers short, and if you do not know something, say, “I do not know; I will confirm by Friday,” and write it down. Composure here is not a performance. It is evidence that you are in control of the project.

A worked example of the follow-up

Within 24 hours, send a written summary: the overrun, its causes, the three options with their effects on cost, coverage and returns, your recommendation, and a consent form. Include the revised budget and a note of what you will report more often from now on. Two investors ask questions. You answer both in writing to all investors, so everyone has the same information. Five of six sign within a week; the agreement’s majority threshold is met, and the sixth’s deemed consent applies after ten days.

If an investor refuses

Suppose one investor, holding 20 percent of the equity, says he will not consent and will not fund his share. Do not argue on the call. Ask, “What would you need to see to support one of these options?” and write down the answer. Then check the agreement: does consent need a majority or unanimity, and what happens to an investor who does not fund a capital call? Many agreements dilute a non-funding investor or let others fund in his place, which Week 69 will cover in detail. Your job in the room is not to force him. It is to understand his objection, give him the information he needs and follow the agreement exactly.

What not to promise to win consent

Under pressure to get signatures, sponsors sometimes promise things they cannot deliver: no further overruns, a guaranteed return, a fee waiver that has not been thought through. Do not. Every promise you make in that meeting becomes a statement investors will quote back to you. Promise only what you control: the reporting, the process and your own conduct. If you want to offer a concession, such as deferring part of your fee, price it first, as JAX taught on Day 3, and put it in writing.

After the meeting

Update your decision journal the same evening: what you decided, what you expected, and what you would do differently. In a year you will want to know whether reporting the design risk earlier would have changed anything, and only a contemporaneous note will tell you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is delaying bad news until the quarterly report, so investors learn of it late and wonder what else is late. The control is a reporting trigger: any cost or schedule change above a set threshold is reported within a week.

The beginner's mistake

Opening with the explanation rather than the number. Investors cannot weigh a story until they know how big it is.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the hostile question: acknowledge, bridge, answer, and “I’ll confirm by Friday.” This meeting used all of it. When an investor asks what else could go wrong, acknowledge the concern, bridge to the cost-to-complete forecast, and answer with the next largest risks by name.

Recap

Lead with the number, own the cause, offer priced options with a recommendation, and say what will change. Stay silent after the number and after the options. Follow up in writing to everyone within a day.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: Week 68 review, with Cole’s Auditor’s Chair.
checklist: I led with the bottom-line number.
I stated the cause and owned my part of it.
I offered priced options and a clear recommendation.
I told investors what will change in reporting from now on.
I stayed silent after the number and after the options.
I said “I will confirm by Friday” for anything I did not know.
I sent a written summary and consent form to all investors within a day.
I gave every investor the same information.
head: Field checklist
speak: At a quarterly meeting with bad news, I lead with the number. The steel package is 1,500,000 dollars over budget; contingency covers 600,000, and the remaining 900,000 takes us 3 percent over the approved budget, which needs your consent. Then I own the cause: a design change for fire requirements and a supplier price increase, and I should have flagged the design risk in March. Then I give priced options: new equity in proportion, a larger loan that cuts our coverage headroom from about 8 to about 5 percent, or finish savings, with my recommendation and a table. I tell them what changes now: big change orders reported within a week. I stay silent after the number and after the options. I never call it normal, never blame by name and never treat the consent as a formality. Within a day, every investor gets the same written summary and consent form.
terms: Reporting trigger — a threshold that requires a cost or schedule change to be reported to investors at once rather than at the next regular report.
Contingency — money held in the budget for unforeseen costs, which is part of the cost, not spare cash.
Majority consent — approval by investors holding a stated share of the equity, as the agreement defines.

hostile.q: You knew about the design change in March. Why are we hearing about the cost now?
hostile.a: You are right, and I should have reported the cost risk in March. At the time, our estimate was that contingency would absorb it, and I did not test that estimate hard enough. That is my mistake. From this quarter, every change order above 250,000 dollars will be reported to you within a week, with its effect on contingency and on the budget.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 68 Review: Governance, Reporting and Alignment
summary: Six questions on investors and joint ventures, a recap of the week, Cole’s Auditor’s Chair on a hypothetical quarterly investor report, and a two-minute boardroom explanation. Answer each question aloud before you read the answer.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: investors give you their money and their trust in exchange for a written list of decisions they control, honest reporting on a fixed schedule, and proof that you win only when they do.

Recall

Q. How do you test whether a sponsor is aligned with investors?

A. Model the sponsor’s total earnings in a good and a bad case. If fees cushion the sponsor far more than investors, alignment is weak.

Q. Why is splitting the difference dangerous in a negotiation?

A. Because the midpoint is set by whoever anchored more aggressively, not by value, and it can land beyond your limit.

Q. What records make shareholder financing in a structure defensible to an auditor?

A. Signed loan agreements, arm’s length terms, payments that match the schedule, and board approvals, kept together.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will raise equity many times in your career, and each raise is easier if the last group of investors would back you again. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you are ready to negotiate a joint-venture agreement. Answer each aloud first.

The six questions

Question 1. What is a major decisions list?

Answer: A defined set of actions, such as budget changes above a tolerance, borrowing, selling and related-party contracts, that need investor consent. Everything else stays with the sponsor.

Question 2. State Rule 68.

Answer: Disclose every related-party arrangement, get investor approval before it starts, and never give yourself control that no investor can check or remove.

Question 3. In the good case the sponsor earned about 2,530,000 dollars and in the bad case about 1,420,000. What does that tell an investor, and what is the fix?

Answer: Fees cushion the sponsor much more than the investors. Defer part of the development fee and subordinate the asset management fee behind the preferred return.

Question 4. What is a corporate opportunity, and what do you do when you find one?

Answer: An opportunity that may belong to the venture because of your role. Disclose it and let the investors decide in writing before you act.

Question 5. How do you check a promote from an investor report?

Answer: Roll investor capital forward at the preferred rate, subtracting each distribution on its date, subtract that from exit cash, split the remainder and compare with what was paid.

Question 6. What is the first thing you say at a meeting with bad news?

Answer: The number, and whether investors must decide anything. Then the cause, the options and what changes.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

JAX set the frame: major decisions, reporting, alignment and removal for cause. Ford and Cole took WeWork in 2019, where disclosure revealed related-party dealings and unchecked control, giving Rule 68. JAX priced fees against promote. Omar explained fiduciary duties, conflicts, information rights and consent. Nadia rebuilt a waterfall backward and found an overpaid promote. JAX ran the quarterly meeting with bad news.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 68 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole’s Auditor’s Chair: read this hypothetical quarterly investor report as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Quarterly Report, Q3. Construction is progressing well and we remain confident in the business plan. Cost: budget 30,000,000 dollars; spent to date 16,500,000; remaining budget 13,500,000. Contingency is healthy. Change orders this quarter were approved in the ordinary course. Our affiliate, Sponsor Build Ltd., continues as contractor. Lease-up is expected to start on schedule. Distributions: promote of 150,000 dollars was paid to the Sponsor in advance of exit, as agreed informally with the lead investor. Signed: the Sponsor.

The defects. First, it reports remaining budget, not cost to complete, so it cannot show whether the project is in balance. Second, contingency is described as healthy with no figure and no statement of how much has been used. Third, change orders are approved in the ordinary course with no amounts, so the auditor cannot tell whether the major-decision threshold has been crossed. Fourth, the affiliate contractor is mentioned without the related-party disclosure, pricing evidence or consent that Rule 68 requires. Fifth, a promote has been paid before exit, before investors have received their capital and preferred return, on an informal agreement with one investor, which breaches the waterfall and treats investors unequally. Sixth, schedule and leasing claims have no dates or evidence, and the report is signed only by the sponsor, with no independent review.

Then the auditor asks for the evidence: the cost-to-complete forecast and the monitor’s report; the contingency log; every change order with its amount and approval; the related-party schedule, bids and consents; the written amendment, if any, authorising an early promote, signed by all investors; and the schedule with its critical path. A report that cannot produce this list is not a report; it is a hope.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a new investor who asks, “Why should we trust you with our money?” Then compare with this model.

Model answer: “Because you will not have to trust me blindly. Before you invest, we agree a business plan and a list of major decisions that need your consent: budget changes beyond 3 percent, borrowing, selling, new partners and any contract with my companies. You get a quarterly report in a fixed format, with cost to complete, contingency used, schedule and loan tests, plus annual statements reviewed by an independent accountant, and any big change within a week. I invest 10 percent alongside you on the same terms. My promote is paid only after you receive your capital and an 8 percent preferred return, and part of my fees waits behind that too. Every related-party contract is disclosed, priced against independent bids and approved by you first. And if I commit serious misconduct, you can remove me.”

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you cover decisions, reporting, alignment and removal? Did you finish in two minutes?

How to use this review

Take one real joint-venture agreement, from a past deal or a public example, and mark four things in it with a pen: the major decisions list, the reporting clause, the alignment terms and the removal clause. Then write one sentence beside each saying what it protects and what it costs the sponsor. Next, take any investor report you have received and read it in the Auditor’s Chair: for each statement, write the evidence you would ask for. Finally, rebuild one waterfall backward from actual cash flows, as Nadia did, and check whether the promote matches. Each exercise takes under an hour, and together they cover the whole week.

Then record the boardroom drill on your phone and listen to it once. Mark where you hesitated. Those hesitations are the points to study again before you sit in front of a real investor.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a sponsor who treats investor rights as paperwork: informal side agreements, early promotes and undisclosed affiliates. The control is to follow the agreement to the letter, in writing, for every investor equally.

The beginner's mistake

Agreeing something informally with the lead investor and assuming the others will not mind. They will, and the agreement usually requires them to be treated equally.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya and Roman taught that cost to complete, not budget remaining, decides whether a construction loan is in balance. Today the Auditor’s Chair applied the same test to an investor report. The lender and the investors are asking the same question about the same building, and your report must answer it for both.

Recap

Major decisions, reporting, alignment and removal, settled in writing before the money arrives. Rule 68 for related parties and control. Fees tested against promote. Waterfalls rebuilt from cash. Bad news early, with a number, a cause and a choice.

Next: JAX, with LEX, on First Principles: partner agreements, vesting, deadlock and what happens when a partner leaves.
checklist: Answer: what a major decisions list is.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was about investors and joint ventures. Investors give me capital in exchange for four things in writing: a major decisions list that says what they must approve, a fixed reporting schedule with cost to complete and covenant tests, alignment through co-investment, a promote paid only after their capital and preferred return, and fees partly deferred behind that, and a clear right to remove me for cause. I test alignment by modelling my earnings in a good case and a bad case. I follow Rule 68: disclose every related-party arrangement, get approval before it starts, and never hold control no one can check. I know the law of the vehicle may give me fiduciary duties, so I disclose opportunities before acting. I rebuild every promote backward from actual cash flows before it is paid. And when the news is bad, I give investors the number first, then the cause, the options and what changes.
terms: Auditor’s Chair — reading a document as a hostile auditor would, asking for the evidence behind each statement.
Side agreement — an informal arrangement with one investor outside the main agreement, which can breach equal treatment.
Equal treatment — the principle, often written into the agreement, that investors of the same class receive the same rights and information.

hostile.q: An auditor asks: why was a promote paid before exit, and who authorised it?
hostile.a: It should not have been. The agreement pays the promote only after investors receive their capital and preferred return, and an informal understanding with one investor does not change that. I have returned the 150,000 dollars to the project account, and I am sending all investors a written explanation this week. Any future change to the waterfall will be made by a written amendment signed by every investor whose consent the agreement requires.
